title: Jaylen Waddle's strong start and other takeaways from Week 1 of Broncos OTAs | Altitude Advantage
text: Welcome into another edition of Altitude Advantage. I'm your host, Eric Dala, joined by a couple of special guests this afternoon following the first week of Broncos OTAAS. The Hall of Famer Steve Atwater is in the studio with us. >> Let's do it. AD >> Steve. And then we got uh Susanna Weir, contributor now. >> Yeah. >> Not going anywhere. >> There we go. Here to stay. So, uh we've got a lot to to talk about today. We just saw for the first time the first open practice of Broncos otaas. Steve, it's the first time we've seen these guys on the field since the end of last season when the team made it to the AFC Championship game. Um, so much to be proud of from a year ago. A 14-3 record. First AFC West title since 2015, the number one seed. You host the AFC Championship game, but it's done. It's over. You got to start again. And we heard Pat Certam say that earlier this week when he talked at his community event that that none of that matters, Steve, from from your perspective, and you've had to do it a bunch of times where you had a good season, you made it to a Super Bowl, you had an extended playoff run, but then you got to turn the page. How difficult is that? And what is this time of year like for these guys? Yeah, it's not really difficult, but I think um you know there maybe just a little bit of disappointment but also, you know, pride and and knowing that they played so well and nobody was really giving them a chance at the beginning of the season, but um you know, now uh you got to turn the page and uh each year you have to do that win, lose or draw, even if you win, you still got to come back and and and hey, get into a whole different mindset. So, um I from from listening to u coach Peyton talk and also to the players, it seems like, you know, they they've kind of put that behind them and they're ready to start a new. And it's it's so difficult to start right from the beginning. You got so dagone far and then you got to start right back over at the beginning at the starting line. >> And I think for me like watching one of the difficult things is is that oh there's I'm like let's just get to week one, right? Like there's so much if you're a fan or you're covering the team, there's so much you're like, I just want to see games or like I just want to like I think of um what it must be like for for Buffalo or Baltimore where you're in the playoffs every single year and you're probably like let me just get back to the postseason. You almost want to fast forward through um through the regular season. But but these guys have to be really about the process. And I'd imagine, Steve, that kind of is what separates teams that continue to have success versus teams that are maybe a one-year wonder and find themselves taking a step back the next year. >> Yeah. And I think the team is wellrun. Uh Shawn Peyton, he he's been here before and he's not going to uh let the team do something that he shouldn't do. you know, I think he's leading us uh leading leading the team in the right direction. Uh with the mentality, uh you know, changing up practice schedules and uh you know, some of the offseason stuff is quite different than what it normally was because they went uh deep into the playoffs. So, I think we got the right people in place and uh from the way they're drafting and you know, the free agents that we're signing, every time you hear them talk, man, it's they're impressive. They're they're are impressive individuals, not just players on the field, but but but people and um you know, I I love that this team is built around uh great people because I think you can go further. >> Yeah, absolutely. I think we've we've already seen Taloo Fungo was on the podium today. He's wearing a shirt. It's a GTD, go the distance. Last year, obviously, they didn't quite get to where they wanted to go. It's a focus. It's a it's a mentality, I think, like something that they've always got to be thinking about. and and we'll get to this and Suz, you and I talked about this with the schedule. >> It's hard not to be focused right away because of the way that the year starts. So maybe >> it starts with a bang. >> So So maybe that's a good thing for this team is like, hey, we want to get back to that point. We've got to be ready to go with Casey and then five straight games against playoff teams. It was our first time seeing Jaylen Wadd, the big time trade acquisition, the first time we saw him on the field as soon as we heard him talk. Sean Payeyton talked about him, Courtland Sutton, even Talanohu Funa from a defensive perspective. Kind of what stood out to you in terms of what we heard about Jaylen Wadd and our first impressions of him on the field. >> Yeah, I think um just listening to him talk about how he's just been embraced by this wide receiver room immediately. And not only that, especially uh looking at Bo too, he said, "I've already started to develop a relationship with Bo." and obviously very early, still far out from the season, but developing that relationship and chemistry with them early is very important. And then uh listening to Court talk about him, you know, he said he's fast, he's explosive. Um and then listening to him describe his own game. He said he said use the word exciting, which I liked. Um and so, you know, obviously fans have been waiting to see him on the field. Everybody's been waiting to see him on the field. And so just to see him out there and and hear him talk about how exciting it is to finally start getting work in, start getting reps in with these guys. Um it was an exciting start. And Sean Payton said he's had a great week and um obviously that's only going to continue to build as we look ahead to the season. So >> yeah, Sean talking about the vision, it's could be outside in, it could be inside out, but they they when they made this trade, they knew how they wanted to use him. So it's not like he gets here and you've got to figure it out. Like they've got an idea of how they're going to use Jaylen Wadd I think for a first time play caller in in Davis Web. That's got to be exciting to have a guy like Jaylen Wadd that you can you can use in some different ways. Um Steve, I know the comparison is not one to one necessarily, but like the combination here in 2014 2015 with of DT and Emanuel. Any similarities there between Courtland kind of the big body and Jaylen who can those yards after catch the the quick explosiveness? >> Yeah, I hadn't really thought about that. Yeah. And Emanuel was uh one of those receivers that was was speedy. uh he would lay out for passes. He took some shots too uh a couple of times. Uh but uh his work ethic was off the charts, Emanuels was. And uh I think Jaylen Wald is is kind of built from that same cloth. Um you know, we'll see probably see him in between uh reps when he's not in. He'll be catching passes from uh some of his some of his teammates or coaches or trainers or somebody. and um I I think he's going to be a a big addition to this team, that explosive piece. Uh and we we did we had some explosive plays last year, too. Don't get me wrong, we didn't have any, but I think we'll have more explosive plays with a player uh like Jaylen Wilder with his talents. >> Yeah, I think that it's that explosiveness and like the the quick burst that excites me. And obviously like Marvin, Troy, they do that from a a kind of a deep shot perspective, right? But it's different with Jaylen in terms of how quick he is off the line of scrimmage. Sean Peyton's talked about how quickly he stops. Um, and I just love that like Court and Jaylen are not the same player. They both do different things and do them really well. And then the other thing too is like, okay, stop Courtland and Jaylen Wadd. Now the run game that has a healthy JK Dobbins, RJ Harvey, you add Jonah Coleman. Um, to me it feels like one of the more complete offensive skill groups this team has had in a long time. And obviously you still got to go do it, but you kind of start looking and I always think about, okay, which which guys are going to be headaches for defensive coordinators when you're game planning. And now you've got some headaches, right? Whether it's >> serious headaches. And then you throw in, hey, I believe the tight ends are going to be more active in this offense this year. And if you throw that in there, I think it the the possibilities are limitless. >> Yeah. And Suz, we heard court talk about the tight ends, too, because I think there is this perception locally, nationally, that that you didn't quite get what you thought you were going to get out of Evan a year ago, Evan Ingram. Um, and then maybe Triman doesn't have the national name recognition, but but Court was like, these guys were are doing what they're asked to do. So, he he was pretty strong about that group, too. >> Yeah, absolutely. I mean, he he said exactly right, like they're doing their jobs, and that's what we expect from them, and that's what we've seen from them. And I love that when you asked him about how him and Jaylen compliment each other. He went into like a whole speech about how, you know, having both of them now as threats is just going to open up the rest of the offense. He listed off all the running backs and then went into talking about the tight ends and just um how, you know, having two receivers like that is going to open up so much more and just allow everybody else to take that extra step, whether it be the tight ends or or the running backs having a full healthy room there as well. And not to mention that the the benefit of having the, you know, Jaylen Wadd um he may also spark something in some of our younger players that oh man, I didn't know that's how you did that. And because we got some young players on this team who still have a ton of potential that had, you know, they they they've shown some, but they haven't reached their peak of potential. And I think that having Jayden Wall in the room is just going to be an added benefit to the to those players. Just learning from him, uh, his route run ability and like they said, he makes everything look like it's a goal. >> And if they can learn, imagine you got three or four receivers doing doing that, how potent you're going to be. >> Yeah. There's definitely some like natural ability, right, of how fast he can stop. But but I do think you're right. Like Troy Franklin, he was he took a huge step last year, but I think there's still more there. And you you think about Pat Bryant who did a lot as a rookie and had some really impressive games, but you've got to imagine he's going to take a step. And then Marv, you know, does he get more opportunities like when you when he has those opportunities, he takes advantage and and so um a lot of guys there that that could learn from Jaylen Wadd. I think the the toughness, the mentality, him battling it out with Certan, like those are going to be fun things to watch in training camp. Um, Steve, last thing on Waddle. We heard from Huff that and in part because of what you talked about there that every route looks the same. It makes it really challenging on the back pedal in terms of when to break down and when to when to go pursue. From your perspective, just what sort of bind does that put you in as a safety? >> Well, as a safety, like >> maybe not you cuz you're a Hall of Famer, so you know. >> No, but for me, like I I wouldn't I wasn't looking at his feet. Okay. You know, I I'm looking at what's going on in the back field. If he's running full speed, guess what? I gotta I can't be in my back pedal. >> Yeah, >> because I I wasn't that fast. I wasn't as fast as Huff was. I won't be in my backpedal. If he's five yards away from me, I got to be running speed. >> But but I can imagine um players, you know, different players have different ways of of of of uh playing uh defenses. And if that's something that you're looking at, you know, if if he's, you know, looking like making it look like he's running full speed, then it's going to put you in a bind. Now, corn, I would imagine it's more difficult on cornerbacks because they're they're on those guys all the time. But yeah, as a safety, if if you're looking at his feet, he's too close to you. >> Yeah. Yeah. He's already gone. There's the old saying, right? Like if he's even, he's leaving. >> Yeah. He's gone. >> Yeah. Uh, and I I I would think too like if you're even thinking about it, it's it's costing you a half a second that maybe with as fast as he is out of his break, maybe it's costing you a split second as a safety that, hey, now you're down there to close in on him and he's got an extra 5, 10 yards after the catch. Um, so even that, I'd imagine, is a benefit. So, I really cannot wait to see him. Um, it feels like so long since the trade. It was only just a couple of months, but but finally get to see him on the field. That's exciting. Um, sticking with Huff who last year was a captain for this team. He's going into year two on this defense. Steve, they did so many things well, but I think it is a little bit easy to forget that until the toward the end of last season, and maybe it's because that Buffalo game, they forced so many turnovers that that you kind of forget, but yeah, they didn't have that many, >> but there were not that many going into the second half of the season. I remember Shawn Payeyton saying after the by-week, if if we're going to do what we want to do, one of the things that has to improve is the turnover margin. And it seems like that's a big focus. Um, if they can get that going, Steve, how much better can they be? >> Man, um, they they were amazing last year. And, uh, that was without a ton of turnovers. Uh, and I know Huff puts a lot of that pressure on himself, but it was it it that wasn't the reason they didn't have a lot of a lot of turnovers. That's that's going to happen sometimes. Hope he's not too hard on himself about that. Um, but I also like that, hey, he's he's um, you know, taking responsibility for saying, hey, we we're going to get better. We're working on this, uh, because if you put turnovers in there with the number of sacks that they had, man, can you imagine how how many more opportunities the offense would have had to score points and and how many we would have the wreck would have been better than it was. I I wonder just a little bit, and this is not like a a bad thing, but if there were so many sacks, if like sometimes Bonito and Cooper are getting there too quick, you know, like maybe maybe there's not a chance for a for a takeaway. But I think with Huff, the thing I like is, hey, if your best players are holding themselves accountable and saying, I wasn't good enough, I've got to be better. That's like finding the the extra room in the margins where like it's hard to be a 14 and three team and a top three defense and get even better. If your best players are saying, >> "No, I could have I could have caught half those interceptions. I'm going to get on the Jugs machine and fix that. And and he did say his wrist as he was coming back from that injury that happened the year before. Um that that was part of it. But if your best players, your Certans, your Huangas, your Sutton, um you know, and obviously there's there's a lot more Quinn Miners, like a bunch of all pros on this team. Um if they're saying I can get better in this way, >> that's got to help. Um, Suz, in terms of listening to both Huff and then guys like Court, um, and hearing from Shawn Payeyton, just it does feel like there's that mentality of like what what more can we do? And maybe that goes back to the the go the distance sort of mentality. >> Yeah, absolutely. I think when you achieve this level of success, obviously making just small little adjustments can be what puts you over the top. And so that seems to be the mentality going back to what we were talking about at the beginning of just like we got to start from scratch now. It's good to look back on what we did, but where can we make those extra little adjustments? I think the turnovers are huge. I know early in the season you had some wins that you lost the turnover margin, but still were able to pull out the wins. That's obviously not always the case. I think the stats would indicate that it usually goes the opposite way. And unfortunately, >> yeah, and I mean, looking back at the 2024 season, I feel like turnovers were like the bread and butter of this defense. And so if they can find a way to kind of get back to that, um, you know, that could be that small adjustment that maybe just takes you a little bit further, helps you go the distance. >> Yeah, I I think it'll it will do just that. Um, because they they play so well in in in just about every category, and if you add on, man, a a turnover or two uh each game, man, that's that's huge. >> Yeah. No, no doubt about it. I I think sometimes you see a defense that gets a ton of turnovers and it kind of hides like how good that defense actually is. So I think it's almost better for the Broncos that they were that good without the turnovers because it's like no this is legit. They're get they're forcing punts. They're stopping teams in the red zone. Like they're getting stops. This is not fluky in any way. But then if you can get the turnover margin back to kind of closer because they were they were near the bottom of the league for a while in terms of that category. Ended up getting better as a season went on. Like if Certan can get a couple more picks or Riley Moss can get a couple more picks, um Huff catches a few, Brandon Jones, like you add those in, maybe a few more. There were a lot of sacks last year, not a ton of force fumbles. You had some of those in. Now you're talking about a team that one, Suz, I think you're right, that like the turnover battle, maybe you win more, the turnover battle more often, which you might need in some of those early games against really good teams. But then I also think that that maybe helps you. Last year the Broncos won so many one-score games. If you're playing a team that you should beat and you're beating maybe a turnover or two, it makes it a 14-point game or a 20point game and and you can you can kind of >> breathe a little >> breathe a little bit. You can you can uh you can relax. You don't have to have a you know freak out at the end of the game. And so um >> that would I I think help. And I do think that the point about the turnover margin is interesting. But it's also, I think, a good sign that when you lose the turnover battle and you still win, probably means you've got a pretty good football team. And so if again, if you put yourself on the the side where you're winning the game or where you're winning the turnover margin and you're still playing well, maybe you put some of these out of reach, um Steve, you don't have to be standing there at the end of the game and we're we're shaking the desk trying to figure out what's going to happen. >> Like, come on, we can do it. >> So that that would definitely help. Um, just a few other things we heard from Shawn Payeyton on this uh, what day is it? Thursday. He uh, he said no joint practices this year because the team because they advanced so far in the postseason a couple days behind from an installation standpoint. They need those extra days. Steve, I don't know how much in your career you did the the joint practice thing. >> We did them a couple times. One one time over in Tokyo, one of the hottest days of my life. I remember in practice uh um, I I was I had to get some water and I looked over to the sideline. and the trainer, he has some he was squeezing water over top of his head, too. I was like, "Man, it's a hot day out here." Um, but yeah, it's um it's it it does take some time. It does take a little bit of more energy out of you. And if you got some other things that you need to get done, then hey, you you just can't do it. And you know how organized Shawn is, you know, he he's got he's got this stuff down to the hour. >> Yeah. Well, and I think that that's exactly right is that Shawn Peyton has earned the benefit of the doubt in terms of how to handle this team, how to coach this team. And if he's saying we join practice isn't what this team needs, this team needs more practices as a group. And then, hey, get maybe maybe the starters play a few more reps in the preseason games, then, you know, I'm right there being like, okay, I buy it. Because everything has worked the last few years in terms of how to handle this, how to take this team from where they were to where they are. He's won a world championship. So, I think this is one of the the situations where Yeah. Is it is it fun as a from our perspective to see like who are the preseason games against this year? Like you got Atlanta. Would it be fun to see uh Certan and Drake London go up against each other? Yeah, of course it'd be fun. But like if if what's best for the team and what they need to be ready for week one um then it feels obvious to me. >> Yeah. No, I'm I'm with you on that. Um you know, he's he's earned that right and he's got credibility, a ton of it. Yeah. Uh the other thing we heard is um that Bo Nicks obviously didn't practice this week. Sounds like maybe could still practice during mini camp, which is in a couple weeks. We we'll see kind of the extent of that. Um Shawn Payeyton did say he's been throwing before practice, so that's encouraging to hear. And we know that Bo wants to be out there. We've heard we heard Sean say that a few weeks ago of, hey, we're going to be holding him back. We're going to be being smart. Um again, the expectation is full go for training camp. We'll be ready to go. um and may see him even in mini camp in a couple weeks. So, we will keep everybody updated on that. But, uh yeah, a lot that we learned in week one of OTAAS. We saw Jaylen Waddle on the field for the first time. Uh heard from Telenoa Hufunga about this defense, what they can do to be even better and a whole lot more. So, stay tuned to denver broncosc.com for additional coverage. But for the Hall of Famer Steve Atwater and Broncos.com Susanna Wear, I'm Eric Dala. Thanks for listening.

title: Jaylen Waddle on joining Broncos’ WR corps: ‘It’s a great group, honestly’
text: Jaylen, how's everything going for you so far? How nice is it to be on the field with your new teammates? >> Um, it's been good, man. It was a beautiful day. Uh, got to go out and compete. U, so any anytime you get a chance like that is, um, always a blessing. >> How great is it having a guy like Pat Certan maybe helping guide you, give you advice, and how things work around, all that? >> Uh, yeah, it was a great, especially like being new in the city, it's um, great to have someone that's been here um, show me around the town. I don't know. He's been great helping me um pick where I'm going stay at, things like that. So, Pat and Bo, they've been on it. >> Jaylen, they gave up pretty good hall of draft picks to get you. Do you feel a little bit like a hired gun? >> Uh, no. No, no, not necessarily. Um, I'm just out here just trying to make plays um with a great group of guys and u yeah, just having fun honestly. What have your initial just conversations, interactions with Bo been like and you know do you see similarities in him as a competitor? How do you think he'll end up fostering that relationship? >> Yeah, Bo is definitely a competitive. He loves talking ball. Um he loves just being around u being around the guys. Um I think he's going to be a a great leader. I can just see the traits um from him just dayto day and everything. And if he sees something, he's going to tell me about it and then we kind of pick each other brains and and try to get on the same page as best we can. What are your initial thoughts of the wide receiver room and how much competition can push this this group this year? >> Man, it's a great group. Um, honestly, and I'm not even talking about, you know, everyone know they can, you know, play and do all these amazing things on the field. I'm just talking about them as people come in as the the new guy and then they welcome me with open arms. Um, treat me like a brother since day one. And, you know, I really got to um look at Court and see what he did with the young guys. And, um, yeah, man, it's it's great. They're great. Jen, how would you describe your game to Broncos country? >> Um, I would say just um fast, physical, um, and, uh, exciting um, honestly. So, yeah. >> Sean talks a lot about vision for players and identifying that. Like, how quickly does he outline for you when you get here what he wants your role to look like, what he wants your impact to look like, or do you sort of learn that as you go along through an offse? I think kind of something that you um you you earn and build and um you know days like this having them bank reps you kind of get to see where you going to be. So um not something necessarily you got to talk about something that you got to you know go out there and do and consistently do on it daily. >> That chemistry takes a long time to develop. How long do you think it'll take you and Bo once Bo gets on the field to kind of get that going so you guys feel comfortable this season? >> Um you know Bo's a tremendous player. Um he's a playmaker. He makes a lot of plays. So, um, when you got a guy like that slinging the ball, I don't think it's going to be, you know, um, take that much time. >> Huff said that Huff said that you have the ability to kind of disguise routes, you know, whether it's a go route or you're going short. I mean, not to give away state secrets, but how do you do that? I mean, >> um, I can't really give away the sauce like that, but, uh, you know, it's definitely a trait, something that, um, a lot of receivers have. Um, I think it's just, um, marrying up your routes. um honestly making everything look like um a go or making you know one route look like the other. So kind of game inside the game. >> What is it like working with Davis Webb, a guy who was just in the league a few years ago? How has he does he have that presence of a coordinator? Does it feel like >> um done? >> Um yeah man, D Web has been great. Um he's still got that player type attitude. You can kind of see in meetings. Um he's real competitive. He gets after us. He challenges us on and off the field. So, um he's been great. >> How does Courtland's game complement you and how do you maybe work off him? >> Well, Courtland's a elite playmaker. Um so, anytime you have a playmaker on the other side of you, it just makes it easy. Someone that the defense have to be um looking for and um and vice versa. U so yeah, >> you guys you guys are going to start right away at Kansas City in five straight games against playoff teams from a year ago. How much do you relish kind of getting right into it facing that high level of competition your first few games as pro? >> Uh yeah, man. We got a a good schedule um against good competition. So, it really get to challenge us um early and early in offense. So, we get to see where we at early. >> What sort of message or takeaway is there when passer Tan gets the pay raise without any drama, not any hold out and the team just does the right thing? What kind of takeaway is there in the locker room? >> Um that >> it's honestly not no takeaway. Um Pat is a tremendous player. Um consistent player. Um a great person and uh yeah man I'm happy for him. >> Does it tell you anything about this ownership group? >> Uh yeah I mean you can say that but u you know it's all with the all with the players and his playmaking ability and you know

title: Mike Green Joins The Lounge | Baltimore Ravens
text: Welcome into the lounge. I'm Ryan Mink here with Cliff Brown and we are thrilled to sit down with Mike Green who is a multi-time friend of the lounge this off season. Joined us at Evb Bank Stadium before the draft and now comes in again. Thank you, Mike. Appreciate the time, man. >> Yeah, man. I appreciate you. >> So, a lot of people are excited about year two for you. you know, I think got a lot of great experience during your rookie season out there, but now it feels like year two, man, we could really see another step from you. How do you approach this season? >> Yeah. So, like, of course, um, after having that long rookie year. >> Yeah. >> Um, I I think now I had a little bit more time to actually be able to gather a lot of more information that, you know, like I was missing my rookie year cuz, you know, I feel like a lot of things move fast your first year in the league. And um I I think coming into this second year, things are starting to slow down for me a lot more and uh I'm getting lot better a lot of a better feel for a lot of things. So, um yeah, like I'm excited for this year as well. Um I I know that um just throughout the year I'm going to be able to keep stacking and keep stacking. So, I'm excited for it. >> I think a lot of fans don't realize just how challenging a rookie season is. Not only for, you know, you're you're coming into league, it's your first year in the NFL, right? the pinnacle of the sport. But the workload from your college season ends, you jump immediately into training for the combine and all the offse, you know, pre-draft stuff, rolls straight into senior bowl, right? Then you go to the combine, the draft, and it's right into rookie mini camp from there. Like there is no break during your rookie season. Not at all. >> So yeah. Can you can you enlighten fans a little bit about the challenge that that entails? >> Yeah. Uh when they say like your rookie year is the longest year of your life, like it that is no over exaggerating. Like it is the longest year of your life. Um because of course like you just mentioned, you know, you got the senior bowl, you got the combine, um you got the pre-draft, the all the pre-draft stuff, and then you have to go and right after that, you got to come to rookie mini camp and then mini camp and um and then you go take like a little break and their break is a little like less than like a vet break. >> They stay a week after mandatory mini camp. >> Exactly. So um so then right and then right when they come back they're right into training camp. So it's basically like you're on for a whole two years basically is um so um it it was extremely long uh you know short the short answer to that but um I I think >> even though it was such a long year it was the most important year of your career. Um, and I I feel like me honestly, um, I I've been able to to gather a lot of information and learn a lot of things from my rookie year. >> And, uh, I know I I tell the rookies all the time now. I was like, yo, like this is going to be a longest year, but once this year is over, everything slows down from there. >> And, um, you know, I try to share a little light on them about that. And uh so yeah um very very very very very long year but you know happy being you too. >> Yeah. So but but now that's that it's over um you kind of look back on it and be like yo like I think my rookie year was so much more beneficial than what it seemed like. >> Yeah. Coach Anthony Weaver, our defensive coordinator a couple days ago mentioned about making a cutup tape for you and how close you were to having possibly a double digit sack year. uh you knew that obviously it was you doing it, but I'm just curious what went through your mind when you watched it and what do you take away from watching that tape? >> Yeah. Um it's crazy you say that because I feel like after every single game um a player probably remembers maybe five to 10 snaps of that game and uh you don't really realize all the good things and all the bad things that happened on in the game that you've done. title: Drew Petzing Media Availability | June 4, 2026
text: What's going on, guys? >> Good. Obviously had a chance to uh talk to a couple here over the last couple months, but nice to be finally on the field and talking about some football. So, let's light a rip. >> Speaking of that, last time we talked to you, I think was uh combine and you were talking about the the weapons you're inheriting, but from watching them on the video on on video standpoint now that you've got them on the field, I know there's no pads and a few guys still need to get on the field, but just your impressions of of the weapons that you're inheriting and how much fun you might be able to have with some of these pieces. It's been great. I mean, it's been fun out there now. Even in pajamas, you know, I think guys are working hard, trying to come together as a unit, trying to improve as individuals. Uh, there's a lot of talent out there. A lot of guys are playing at a really high level. So, uh, it's been a lot of fun. >> What is your number one like focus this offseason? What's the progression of what you're trying to >> I think the goal is always going to be get better at everything we do. That's me as a coach, that's individuals, as players, that's us as units. Um, I think that's got to be the focus and and certainly now because there's not a game plan or an opponent in the imminent future, I think you can dial in on some of the details of that a little bit better. Um, so that's really kind of where we're honing in on >> like the balance of, you know, you're a new coordinator, so there's new parts of the offense, but a lot of it, I'm sure, is similar. Is there are you starting from level 101 or is there have you found it more advanced like when you started? >> I'd say it's a mix. I say every year you try to start back at the beginning and make sure that you build the foundation. I mean, the nature of the NFL, you're going to have some new faces in the room, coaches and players included, and making sure everybody's on the same page. I think that's a big part of the offseason. Uh, but I I think it's important to start from the beginning and build the right foundation so that when you do get to those higher level conversations or you do get into game plan mode, you're where you want to be. >> Drew, do you do you try to keep, I guess, large chunks in place to make this the transition more seamless, or do you really try to bring in your vocab and and put that on these guys? I >> I think it's a mix. You know, I little bit of a unique situation because there's a number of vets who have played at a really high level. So, I don't want to come in here and rip it all up and and make them learn a entirely new language, but there's going to be tweaks. There's going to be changes, and I think they've done a great job of handling that. >> That center quarterback relationship is so vital for an offense, obviously. What specific things do you do at this time of year to help Jared and Cade build that rapport either on the field or off the field? >> Yeah, I think it's both. I think a lot of those are conversations in the meeting room. You know, we talked about being on the same page, watching tape, watching practice, going back through some stuff. And then on the field, some of that's going to take place naturally because you are doing some of those things where you're in and out of the huddle. You're seeing different looks. You know, our defense is doing a great job of challenging us and making us think through and talk through some stuff. Uh, so it's been great to see that relationship kind of grow. >> How much easier is it for you to have a guy in Jared who's been around for now his 11th season. He's seen it all. There isn't anything a defense can probably throw. And when you're installing an offense with a guy that's seen it all like that, just how much easier is the process overall? >> Uh it it definitely makes the job easier, I think. And it's not just him. You have some vets in the room that have played a lot of football that that I can lean on to coach some things and to say, "Hey, you've done this at a really high level. Saint Paneet, you know, even JMO and Gibby, like, hey, you guys have done some great things. You know, how do you think about this? How do you coach this? Let me hear that in front of the room. Let other guys learn from your experience." And I think they've done a great job of embracing that uh and trying to make the players around them better. What is your process for understanding uh how players in the offense learn best and and how to effectively teach the material at this time of year? >> It's a great question. I think it's something we as coaches might be the most important thing we do and and I feel like my job is to to stay on top of that. The position coaches, you know, do that at a really high level and I love the guys that we got and the way that they're going about that so far this off seasonason. Um but it's, you know, it's an individual thing and you got to, you know, you pull from other experience and other guys you've worked with. you try to get that guy to communicate with you on how he learns best and what he needs from us to be successful. Uh because at the end of the day that's the goal. >> It seemed like it's been like a different sense of urgency after missing the postseason last year. Obviously with the type of players they attracted, you know, just and you coming in, do you feel that? And if so, if you do feel that sense of urgency to get back on track, you know, just how how do you help this team, you know, as far as getting back on track? >> Two-part question. I'll go I'll try to go with the first question first. You know, from an urgency standpoint, I I think that's the nature of the league. I I think you're always there. It's a now league. Like we got to show up. We got to get better. We gota we got to be where we want to be. I think you're always going to feel that to some extent. Um and then my role in that, you know, as kind of we talked about is to be the best version of myself and to push the players and bring out the best in them to make sure I'm growing as a coach and pulling on the right things and learning from the right people. Uh so so far it's been an awesome experience. >> Dan and he said the the plan is Jabir to be kind of the the Delcow back this year. Where do you see from last year to this year the the most room for growth in his role >> for I'm sorry Gibbs? Uh you know I I think it can change as we go. I think a lot of it's going to be dictated by what we're good at as a unit. You know where are we the best? Where are we the most effective? Who are we playing and how do we utilize his skill set uh to build on that and he does so many things at a high level that I don't think there's necessarily a ceiling or a cap on what that could look like. Uh but I think that's going to be dictated a lot by the people around him and how they all pieces all fit together. Last season, this offense wasn't able to access the play action game as much as it probably wanted to. Uh, how much is that an emphasis? How much does that correlate to more deep shots potentially? >> Yeah. And I don't want to to punt on the question, I guess you would say, but it's a little bit of what we just talked about with Gibby. Some of that's going to be dictated by who we're playing, what the matchups are, what we look like in protection. Uh, but it's definitely going to be a big part of who we want to be because that indecision on whether it's run or pass, I think, is so critical to being effective in any offense in the NFL. Um, so and I think it fits the skill set of our quarterback, number one, and it, you know, I think it takes some pressure off the offensive line, which in this league is important. Uh, and it allows you to utilize your skill players in an effective manner on base downs. Um, so it's something we're working on. We're going to continue to get better at. We're going to see how good we can be at it to see how much we want to use it. >> With the physical limitations of these early practices, Drew, what what are your points of emphasis with young in particular, young trench players? >> Yeah, I I think the big thing is the learning aspect, right, of like we're still processing. We're still running different schemes. We're still making sure that we're assignment sound and know where we're going and how we're doing it and and can do it quickly, right? Because the game happens fast. So, I think that's a big part of the offseason is how well can you think? How quickly can you think? And then the third piece of that on the field is how well do you communicate to those around you, right? Like is everybody on the same page? When you see something, are you saying it? And that way the guy next to you can react appropriately. I think that's a big part of what this offseason is because we can't bank and that's just the nature of the rules. >> Drew, you get an opportunity to work with a young quarterback and Luke Altmire. What are some points of emphasis for him and how do you like so far of what he's picked up in early parts of OTA? >> I think the emphasis is very similar what we just talked about with the O line. You know, how quickly can you pick it up? You got to call the plays. You got to get in out of the huddle. You know, at the quarterback position, you're responsible for the 10 other guys. Are they doing what they're supposed to be doing? Are you know when they're not and can you correct it before it matters? You know, I think that's a big part of the process of playing quarterback and something that Jared obviously who's been in the league for such a long time does such a high level that you almost start to take it for granted. and some of the young guys got to get there and to watch him do that I think is great for Luke. I think he's really embraced that. Um and I think that's been kind of the the fun thing to get to work with him. You know, you're building it from the ground up because he doesn't have that foundation right now and so we're trying to set that foundation. I think he's he's embracing that challenge. >> What's the thing he's done that's impressed you most so far? Whether it's leadership behind the closed doors with his arm, anything that >> I think unflapable, I guess would be the word that comes to mind. Like he he every days he's the same guy. He he puts in the same process. He works. He never seems overwhelmed by what we're asking him to do or how we're asking him to do it. and uh he's willing to learn and and to work at it which has been great. >> Dan just said that he he doesn't lack confidence. How have you seen that express itself? I guess >> I think in a lot of the ways that he walks on the field and walks in the meeting room and is willing to answer questions and the way he plays the game, you know, I think there's especially with some young quarterbacks, you can see some nerves in the way that they call plays or get out of the huddle or act post snap. Uh whereas with him, I think he, you know, he has a ton of confidence and ability and you feel that in the way he just goes in and out of the huddle and plays the game. How different has this experience been for you? I mean, the the three previous jobs you came in with new coaching staffs and you're kind of implementing a culture collectively. You kind of step in here and the culture, the foundation's been laid for for years. Is is that make the job easier for you in in some ways? >> I think it goes in both directions. You know, I think obviously that's a big part of what I feel like my role is is to integrate myself into the culture that they've built here because it is so impressive and it has succeeded at such a high level. Um, but I lean on the guys, the staff, and you know, some of these guys I've worked with before or known just from being around the league. And they've been great and kind of helping build me up and make me understand how we do things and how what's expected and and I feel like that's a big part of my growth as a coach and coming into this organization. It's been fun. >> Rams made a big move getting Miles Garrett. What does he do to wreck a offensive coordinator's game plan? >> Uh, I mean, I was in the building with him for three years, so I I saw it firsthand. He's a great player. Uh he I mean kind of like the guys we talked about on this offense. I don't know if there's a weakness in his game. Uh he does so many things at such a high level, plays with such violence. So great player. Uh you know, and we were talking about earlier. I know right now he's not on the schedule. So I hope we're playing him this year. >> What's your view of the wide receiver room as a as an entire unit as a whole? >> Say that one more time. >> Just your your view of the that wide receiver room as a collective unit. >> Yeah, it's a really strong unit.
